strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant gap in LLM-based Verilog generation: optimizing functional correctness and hardware Power/Performance/Area simultaneously rather than applying EDA tools only as external post-processing.

The proposed system is technically coherent. Hierarchical gated rewards ensure syntactic and functional validity before expensive synthesis and PPA evaluation, while CDPO combines per-reward advantage normalization, curriculum-based weighting of process rewards, and prompt-conditioned PPA preferences.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: it covers four 7B base models, VerilogEval Machine/Human, RTLLM v1.1 and v2.0, specialized Verilog systems, proprietary models, reward ablations, comparisons with GRPO/DAPO, PDK/synthesis-tool sensitivity, larger AutoSilicon designs, and runtime analysis.

The main empirical claim is well supported: ChipSeek improves functional pass rates and reduces normalized EDAP across model families, and the ablations indicate that the EDA rewards, curriculum, advantage-level aggregation, and preference vector each contribute.

The appendices strengthen reproducibility by providing the CDPO algorithm, hyperparameters, EDA tool settings, metric definitions, prompt templates, training-stage ablations, and detailed per-design results; the authors also state that code and scripts will be released.

The paper is clearly written and effectively communicates a complex multi-stage training and evaluation pipeline, with informative framework diagrams, learning curves, radar charts, and a concrete barrel-shifter case study.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is mainly integrative. Hierarchical/gated rewards, group-relative advantage normalization, curriculum learning, multi-objective reward weighting, and preference-conditioned prompts are established techniques; the paper does not demonstrate a fundamentally new RL method beyond their domain-specific combination.

Statistical rigor is limited. The tables appear to report single training runs, with no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which is important because RL training and EDA-reported PPA can be unstable.

PPA scores are averaged only over tasks that each model solves successfully, so the denominator and task difficulty can differ across models. A common-solved-subset analysis or penalty for failed designs is needed to rule out survivor bias. The reported maximum EDAP over 10 candidates is also optimistic, although average and minimum values help.

Functional reward quality depends heavily on GPT-5-generated testbenches. The paper says a verification pipeline filters incorrect pairs, but it does not quantify testbench coverage or correctness rigorously, leaving some risk of incomplete tests and reward hacking; held-out benchmark evaluation mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Some broader claims are only partially substantiated. Fine-grained power/delay/area control and improvements across circuit categories are supported by relatively limited analyses, and the authors themselves observe weaker optimization on control and memory modules.

Reproduibility remains constrained by the reliance on proprietary generation APIs, large-scale EDA computation, and an automatically collected web corpus. Although Yosys/OpenROAD and the base models are open, the PDF does not provide an artifact link or enough evidence that the complete generated dataset and filtering pipeline can be reconstructed exactly.

The work is highly domain-specific and does not establish whether the CDPO design transfers to other code-generation or tool-integrated RL tasks, which may limit its broader significance for a general NLP audience.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem for code-generating LLMs: jointly optimizing Verilog functional validity with hardware Power, Performance, and Area rather than treating compilation or test passage alone as success.

The closed-loop EDA-integrated design is practically useful. Hierarchical gating avoids expensive simulation, synthesis, and PPA analysis for invalid designs, while preference vectors enable prompt-level control over power, delay, and area trade-offs.

CDPO is well motivated for multi-objective RL: decoupled group-relative advantage normalization reduces reward-scale interference, curriculum scheduling stabilizes early learning, and preference-conditioned weighting supports target-specific optimization.

The empirical scope is broad for a 7B-model study, including four base models, VerilogEval machine/human tracks, RTLLM v1.1 and v2.0, several recent Verilog-specific systems, reward ablations, and comparisons against GRPO and DAPO.

Additional evidence from cross-PDK/cross-tool sensitivity, timing- versus area-driven synthesis, larger AutoSilicon designs, runtime acceleration, training curves, and a detailed case study strengthens the practical evaluation.

The reported gains are substantial on several benchmarks, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail, prompt templates, evaluation equations, and per-module PPA results. The stated open-source release would further improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is primarily an integration of known techniques—group-relative RL, curriculum annealing, multi-objective reward weighting, and prompt-conditioned preferences—rather than a substantially new RL or language-generation method. This limits main-conference novelty.

Empirical rigor is insufficient for a fully confident state-of-the-art claim: there are no multiple random seeds, training variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and it is unclear whether all baselines were rerun under identical prompts, sampling budgets, EDA versions, and synthesis settings.

The aggregate PPA score can be biased because it averages over tasks for which a model produced at least one functionally correct design. Models that fail harder tasks are not evaluated on them unless an explicit failure penalty is used; results should also be reported on a common task set.

Some headline improvement percentages are not transparently derivable from the printed tables. For example, the reported pass@5 change is 11.36 percentage points but about 15.6% relative, and the claimed EDAP reductions do not directly match the best prior max/avg/min values in Table 2.

The training labels depend heavily on generated artifacts: GPT-5 testbenches, DeepSeek-R1-enriched descriptions, and generated CoT chains. Without test-coverage, mutation testing, or independent validation, incomplete or incorrect testbenches could create reward hacking or weak supervision.

PPA comparisons omit several crucial EDA details in the main text, including clock constraints, operating corners, switching activity, tool versions, and timing-closure criteria. Relative normalization helps, but these details are necessary for reliable hardware interpretation.

The notion of specification alignment is narrower than claimed. In the barrel-shifter example, the prompt explicitly requests mux2X1 submodules, but the generated solution replaces them with behavioral shifts; functional and area objectives are rewarded while structural instruction adherence is not.

Reproducibility gaps remain: no resolvable artifact URL is visible in the reviewed version, and key settings such as dataset URLs/listing, seeds, w_func, the curriculum EMA coefficient, exact EDA commands, and filtering rules are not fully specified. Reliance on proprietary teacher models also complicates reconstruction.

Several claims are overstated: passing generated tests is not proof of functional correctness, and successful Yosys/OpenROAD synthesis does not by itself guarantee timing closure or physical realizability. Figure 1 is also cramped, with overlapping labels and ambiguous model naming.
